problem: Support cannot answer 'what happened to this order' without three tabs and a query nobody trusts; the data lives in four services and no one owns the sequence.

capacity.derivation: writes = 4000/(1+50) ≈ 78.4/s; 78.4 × 1500B × 86400s × 180d ≈ 1830 GB before replication; peak egress = 4000 × 1500B × 8 ≈ 48 Mbps

bottleneck: Fan-in write amplification: every order touches 6 upstream events, so the timeline table takes 6x the write rate of the order table and its index is the first thing to saturate

decisions.title: Read model
decisions.chosen: Materialised timeline table, written by a consumer

rejected.option: Query the four services on read
rejected.why: p99 becomes the slowest dependency, and support reads happen during incidents when those services are already unhealthy
the question is asked about orders from minutes ago

decisions.tradeoff: Duplicated state that can drift; paid for with a reconciler and a drift metric

decisions.title: Transport

rejected.why: no replay, and every consumer reimplements retry
no ordering guarantee within an order, which the timeline needs

decisions.tradeoff: Operational weight of a broker for ordering and replay

decisions.title: Delivery semantics
decisions.chosen: At-least-once with an idempotency key per event

rejected.why: cost and coupling exceed the benefit; duplicates are cheap to absorb here

decisions.tradeoff: Every handler must be idempotent, enforced by a shared helper and a test

decisions.title: Storage
decisions.chosen: Postgres partitioned by month with a retention job

rejected.why: the access pattern is a range scan by order id, and no one on the team operates it
we need an authoritative record, not a search index

decisions.tradeoff: A vertical ceiling we will hit around 4x current load; the partition scheme buys the runway to move

slos.measuredBy: server-side histogram, 30-day rolling window in Prometheus
slos.errorBudgetPolicy: at 50% burn, feature work stops until the budget recovers; at 100%, the on-call owns a written plan

slos.measuredBy: timestamp delta emitted by the consumer per event
slos.errorBudgetPolicy: sustained breach pages the owning team; a 1h breach triggers a postmortem

slos.measuredBy: black-box probe every 30s from two regions
slos.errorBudgetPolicy: fast-burn alert pages immediately; slow burn is reviewed weekly

failureModes.failure: Consumer group rebalances repeatedly under load and lag grows without bound
failureModes.blastRadius: Timeline goes stale for every order; reads still succeed, so nobody notices until support complains
failureModes.mitigation: Bounded processing time per message, heartbeat tuned above the p99 handler time, and a lag-based autoscaler
failureModes.detection: Consumer lag alert at 60s of lag, plus the event-to-visible SLO burn alert

failureModes.blastRadius: Ingest pauses; reads continue from the replica with data up to the failover point
failureModes.mitigation: Consumer retries with backoff against a bounded in-memory buffer, then pauses the partition rather than dropping
failureModes.detection: Write error-rate alert and a replica-lag alert

failureModes.failure: Emits a malformed event schema after a deploy
failureModes.blastRadius: One partition stops advancing; other orders unaffected
failureModes.mitigation: Schema validation at the consumer boundary, dead-letter after 3 attempts, and a contract test in the upstream CI
failureModes.detection: Dead-letter queue depth alert, which is also the first thing the runbook checks

failureModes.failure: Silent drift between the timeline and the source of truth
failureModes.blastRadius: Support answers confidently from wrong data — the worst outcome, because it is invisible
failureModes.mitigation: Hourly sampled comparison against the source services; drift above 0.1% opens a ticket automatically
failureModes.detection: Drift metric with an alert; the number is on the service dashboard, not buried in a job log
